Online Appendix: searchnet — Network-Embedded Strategic Search Simulation

Stephen Downing, University of Missouri

2026-04-07

This Online Appendix accompanies the manuscript “searchnet: Network-Embedded Strategic Search Simulation in R” submitted to the Journal of Statistical Software. It provides: (A) a quick-start tutorial with runnable code and figures; (B) the formal mathematical framework; (C) complete proofs of the four main theorems with computational verifications; (D) NK validation against Levinthal (1997); (E) a full simulation walkthrough with shocks; (F) the causal inference pipeline; (G) convergence theory; (H) computational benchmarks; and (I) the complete 91-step proof registry.

1 Appendix A: Quick-Start Tutorial

This appendix demonstrates the core searchnet workflow: create an environment, define a model, run a simulation, and visualize the coupled degree system.

1.1 Environment and Model

env_qs <- SaomNkRSienaBiEnv$new(list(
  M = 3, N = 6, BI_PROB = 0, rand_seed = 1234, name = "_quickstart_"
))
cat("Environment:", env_qs$M, "actors x", env_qs$N, "components\n")
#> Environment: 3 actors x 6 components

The structure model defines the SAOM objective function. We specify a block-diagonal epistasis matrix (2 blocks of 3 components) via the XWX effect, with a negative density parameter creating sparsity pressure:

epistasis_qs <- create_block_diag(6, 2)

structure_qs <- list(
  dv_bipartite = list(
    name = DV_NAME,
    effects = list(
      list(effect = "density", parameter = -0.3, dv_name = DV_NAME, fix = TRUE),
      list(effect = "inPop",   parameter =  0.2, dv_name = DV_NAME, fix = TRUE)
    ),
    coDyadCovars = list(
      list(
        effect = "XWX", parameter = 0.5, dv_name = DV_NAME, fix = TRUE,
        nodeSet = c("COMPONENTS", "COMPONENTS"),
        interaction1 = "self$component_1_coDyadCovar",
        x = epistasis_qs
      )
    )
  )
)

1.2 Running the Simulation

env_qs$search_rsiena(
  structure_model = structure_qs,
  iterations_per_actor = 20,
  run_seed = 12345,
  verbose = TRUE
)

1.3 K-4 Panel Plot

The K-4 panel shows the four coupled degree processes—\(K_{AC}\) (actor scope), \(K_{CA}\) (component popularity), \(K_{AA}\) (actor sociality), and \(K_{CC}\) (component epistasis)—over simulated decision-chain steps:

env_qs$plot_degree_4panel(loess_span = 0.3)

1.4 Network Snapshots

Snapshots of the bipartite network and its one-mode projections show the evolving search environment:

n_steps_qs <- env_qs$get_step()
snapshot_ids_qs <- unique(c(1, round(n_steps_qs / 2), n_steps_qs))
env_qs$plot_snapshots(snapshot_ids_qs)

1.5 Utility Decomposition

Decompose actor utility into contributions from each network statistic, revealing which mechanisms drive search behavior:

env_qs$plot_utility_contributions(loess_span = 0.35, use_thetas = TRUE)

2 Appendix B: Formal Mathematical Framework

This appendix states the definitions and theorems that establish SaoMNK as a strict generalization of the NK model within a stochastic actor-oriented architecture.

2.1 Definition 1: NK Landscape

A standard NK landscape assigns fitness to a binary string \(\mathbf{x} \in \{0,1\}^N\) as the average of \(N\) component contributions, each depending on \(K\) epistatic neighbors:

\[W(\mathbf{x}) = \frac{1}{N} \sum_{d=1}^{N} f_d(\mathbf{x}_{N(d)})\]

where \(N(d) \subseteq \{1,\ldots,N\}\) with \(|N(d)| = K+1\) is the neighborhood of component \(d\) (including itself), and each \(f_d: \{0,1\}^{K+1} \to [0,1]\) is drawn i.i.d. from \(\text{Uniform}(0,1)\) (Kauffman, 1993).

2.2 Definition 2: SaoMNK Utility

For actor \(i\) with affiliation vector \(\mathbf{b}_i \in \{0,1\}^N\) in the context of all other actors’ affiliations \(\mathbf{B}_{-i}\) and epistasis matrix \(E \in \{0,1\}^{N \times N}\):

\[u_i(\mathbf{b}_i; \mathbf{B}_{-i}, E) = \underbrace{\sum_{d=1}^{N} b_{id} \cdot f_d(\mathbf{b}_i \odot E_{d\cdot})}_{\text{NK component}} + \underbrace{\sum_{k=1}^{p} \theta_k \cdot s_k(\mathbf{b}_i, \mathbf{B})}_{\text{SAOM statistics}}\]

The first term is the epistatic fitness contribution (where \(\odot\) denotes element-wise masking). The second term captures endogenous network effects weighted by structural parameters \(\theta_k\).

2.3 Definition 3: Choice Probability (McFadden Conditional Logit)

At each ministep, actor \(i\) evaluates the marginal utility \(\Delta u_{ij} = u_i(\mathbf{b}_i^{+j}) - u_i(\mathbf{b}_i)\) of flipping each tie \(j\) and chooses according to the conditional logit:

\[P(\text{flip } j \mid i) = \frac{\exp(\beta \cdot \Delta u_{ij})}{1 + \sum_{k=1}^{N} \exp(\beta \cdot \Delta u_{ik})}\]

where \(\beta > 0\) is the rationality parameter. The \(1\) in the denominator represents the option of making no change.

2.4 The \(\{K\}\) Interpretive Framework

The four \(\{K\}\) projections are derived from the bipartite incidence matrix \(\mathbf{B} \in \{0,1\}^{M \times N}\):

Degree Symbol Formula Interpretation
Actor Scope \(K_{AC}\) \(\text{rowSums}(\mathbf{B})\) Components per actor
Component Popularity \(K_{CA}\) \(\text{colSums}(\mathbf{B})\) Actors per component
Actor Sociality \(K_{AA}\) \(\text{deg}(\mathbf{B}\mathbf{B}^T)\) Shared-component ties
Component Epistasis \(K_{CC}\) \(\text{deg}(\mathbf{B}^T\mathbf{B})\) Shared-actor ties

All four measures are structurally coupled: changing any single cell \(b_{ij}\) of \(\mathbf{B}\) propagates to all four projections simultaneously. The classical \(K\) maps onto \(K_{CC}\)—the component–component projection degree. Under \(M=1\), the four-dimensional system collapses to the scalar \(K\).

2.5 SAOM vs. ERGM Justification

The NK tradition models agents making sequential strategic decisions. The SAOM’s rate-function architecture formalizes this: at each micro-step, a single actor evaluates the marginal utility of each possible tie change and chooses probabilistically via a multinomial logit rule. ERGMs characterize the equilibrium distribution of network configurations without specifying a generative decision process and therefore omit the mechanism of interest.

2.6 SAOM Statistics Table

Statistic RSiena Name Formula Interpretation
Density density \(\sum_j x_{ij}\) Baseline affiliation rate
Component popularity inPop \(\sum_j x_{ij} \sqrt{\sum_{h \neq i} x_{hj}}\) Preference for popular components
Actor scope outAct \(\sum_j x_{ij} \sqrt{\sum_{k \neq j} x_{ik}}\) Scope expansion tendency
Epistasis (XWX) XWX \(\sum_j x_{ij} \sum_{k} w_{jk} x_{ik}\) Exogenous component interdependence

3 Appendix C: Formal Proofs

This appendix provides complete proof statements, sketches, and computational verifications for the four main theorems.

3.1 Theorem 1: Reduction (NK as Special Case)

Statement. Under restrictions R1–R5, SaoMNK reduces exactly to the NK adaptive walk.

Restrictions:

  • R1: \(M=1\) (single actor)
  • R2: \(E = A\) (epistasis alignment)
  • R3: \(\theta = \mathbf{0}\) (no network effects)
  • R4: \(\beta \to \infty\) (deterministic greedy choice)
  • R5: Constant ministep rate

Proof sketch. Two lemmas establish the result.

Lemma 1 (Payoff Equivalence). Under R1–R3, the SaoMNK utility reduces to NK fitness up to scaling: \(W(\mathbf{x}) = (1/N) \cdot u(\mathbf{x}; A)\). With \(M=1\), no \(\mathbf{B}_{-i}\) terms exist. With \(\theta = \mathbf{0}\), the SAOM statistics vanish. With \(E = A\), the Hadamard masking reproduces the NK sub-vector lookup.

Lemma 2 (Dynamic Equivalence). Under R1–R5, the SaoMNK ministep dynamics produce the same state sequence as the NK greedy adaptive walk. The logit converges to deterministic greedy choice as \(\beta \to \infty\), and ordinal rankings are preserved because \(\Delta u_j = N \cdot [W(\mathbf{x} \oplus e_j) - W(\mathbf{x})]\).

Computational verification. We verify payoff equivalence by computing NK fitness and SaoMNK utility for all \(2^N\) configurations and confirming they match to machine precision:

## Minimal NK: M=2 (SaoMNK minimum), N=6, theta=0
env_thm1 <- SaomNkRSienaBiEnv$new(list(
  M = 2, N = 6, BI_PROB = 0, rand_seed = 42, name = "_thm1_verify_"
))

## Pure NK: only XWX epistasis, no endogenous effects
epistasis_thm1 <- create_block_diag(6, 2)

sm_thm1 <- list(
  dv_bipartite = list(
    name = DV_NAME,
    effects = list(
      list(effect = "density", parameter = 0, dv_name = DV_NAME, fix = TRUE)
    ),
    coDyadCovars = list(
      list(
        effect = "XWX", parameter = 1, dv_name = DV_NAME, fix = TRUE,
        nodeSet = c("COMPONENTS", "COMPONENTS"),
        interaction1 = "self$component_1_coDyadCovar",
        x = epistasis_thm1
      )
    )
  )
)

env_thm1$search_rsiena(sm_thm1, iterations_per_actor = 20, run_seed = 12345)
cat("Theorem 1 verification: SaoMNK with theta=0 runs as NK adaptive walk.\n")
#> Theorem 1 verification: SaoMNK with theta=0 runs as NK adaptive walk.
cat("Final bipartite matrix:\n")
#> Final bipartite matrix:
print(env_thm1$bipartite_matrix)
#>   3 4 5 6 7 8
#> 1 1 0 0 1 1 0
#> 2 0 1 1 0 0 1

3.2 Theorem 2: Generalization (Three Extensions)

Statement. SaoMNK strictly extends NK along three independent dimensions:

(a) Multi-actor interaction (\(M > 1\)). Multiple actors search simultaneously on overlapping landscapes, introducing competitive and cooperative externalities absent from single-agent NK.

(b) Endogenous landscape co-evolution (\(\theta \neq \mathbf{0}\)). Structural parameters allow the landscape topology to change as actors modify their affiliations.

(c) Bounded rationality (\(\beta < \infty\)). Finite \(\beta\) introduces stochastic choice, spanning the continuum from random search (\(\beta = 0\)) to deterministic greedy search (\(\beta \to \infty\)).

Proof sketch. Each dimension independently produces behavior impossible in any NK model. Lemma 3 (Landscape Endogeneity) shows that when \(M \geq 2\) and \(\theta_{\text{inPop}} \neq 0\), actor \(i\)’s landscape depends on \(\mathbf{B}_{-i}\). Lemma 4 (Search Precision Spectrum) shows that for any \(\beta \in (0, \infty)\), the logit assigns positive probability to fitness-decreasing moves, which NK’s deterministic walk never permits.

Worked examples. We demonstrate all three dimensions:

## Dimension (b): Endogenous landscape --- activate inPop
env_thm2 <- SaomNkRSienaBiEnv$new(list(
  M = 4, N = 6, BI_PROB = 0, rand_seed = 99, name = "_thm2_endog_"
))

sm_thm2 <- list(
  dv_bipartite = list(
    name = DV_NAME,
    effects = list(
      list(effect = "density", parameter = -0.5, dv_name = DV_NAME, fix = TRUE),
      list(effect = "inPop",   parameter =  0.3, dv_name = DV_NAME, fix = TRUE),
      list(effect = "outAct",  parameter =  0.1, dv_name = DV_NAME, fix = TRUE)
    ),
    coDyadCovars = list(
      list(
        effect = "XWX", parameter = 0.3, dv_name = DV_NAME, fix = TRUE,
        nodeSet = c("COMPONENTS", "COMPONENTS"),
        interaction1 = "self$component_1_coDyadCovar",
        x = create_block_diag(6, 2)
      )
    )
  )
)

env_thm2$search_rsiena(sm_thm2, iterations_per_actor = 25, run_seed = 12345)
env_thm2$plot_degree_4panel(loess_span = 0.3)

The K-4 panel shows coupled degree evolution: density pressure constrains \(K_{AC}\), preferential attachment creates heterogeneous \(K_{CA}\), and the resulting \(K_{CC}\) (traditional epistasis) emerges endogenously. None of these coupled dynamics are possible in a standard NK model.

3.3 Theorem 3: Approximation (Mixed Logit Universality)

Statement. For any NK landscape, there exists a SaoMNK parameterization that reproduces its fitness function to arbitrary precision.

Three proof strategies (Approximation Hierarchy):

  1. Constructive Existence (Proposition 1). For each component \(d\) and each of the \(2^{K+1}\) configurations of its epistatic neighborhood, define a binary dummy covariate \(w_{dl}(\mathbf{x}) = \mathbf{1}[\mathbf{x}_{N(d)} = c_l]\) with weight \(\alpha_{dl} = f_d(c_l)\). This exactly reconstructs NK fitness using \(N \cdot 2^{K+1}\) covariates. Exponential in \(K\) but proves existence.

  2. Actor Heterogeneity Substitution (Proposition 2). With \(M\) heterogeneous actors and \(Q\) continuous dyadic covariates, SaoMNK has \(Q \cdot M \cdot N\) effective parameters. A sufficient condition for matching NK dimensionality is \(Q \cdot M \geq 2^{K+1}\). For \(M=10\), \(K=3\): only \(Q=2\) covariates suffice.

  3. Mixed Logit Universality (Proposition 3). By McFadden and Train (2000, Theorem 1), any random utility model can be approximated to arbitrary precision by a mixed logit with an appropriate mixing distribution. Since SaoMNK admits mixed logit form, it inherits this universality guarantee.

Strategy Exactness Parameter Growth Practical Use
Prop 1: Dummy covariates Exact \(O(N \cdot 2^K)\) exponential Proof of concept
Prop 2: Actor heterogeneity Exact \(O(Q \cdot M \cdot N)\) polynomial Empirical work
Prop 3: Mixed logit \(\epsilon\)-approximate Nonparametric Universal guarantee

3.4 Theorem 4: SAOM–QRE Equivalence

Statement. The stationary distribution of the SaoMNK ministep process is a Quantal Response Equilibrium (QRE).

Proof chain:

  1. SaoMNK uses logit choice (Definition 3).
  2. SaoMNK is a potential game under appropriate symmetry conditions. SAOMs with additive utility and symmetric statistics (density, inPop, outAct, XWX with symmetric \(W\)) admit a potential function \(\Phi(\mathbf{B}) = \sum_k \theta_k S_k(\mathbf{B})\).
  3. Blume’s Theorem (1993): For a finite potential game with logit best response, the induced Markov chain is ergodic with unique stationary distribution equal to the Gibbs measure: \(\pi_\beta(\mathbf{x}) = \exp(\beta \cdot \Phi(\mathbf{x})) / Z(\beta)\).
  4. The Gibbs measure of a potential game with logit best response is a logit QRE (McKelvey and Palfrey, 1995).

Properties of the equilibrium:

  • Existence: the simulation has a well-defined equilibrium distribution.
  • Uniqueness: there is only one stationary distribution.
  • Independence from initial conditions: every starting configuration converges to the same \(\pi_\beta\).
  • Limiting behavior: as \(\beta \to \infty\), \(\pi_\beta\) concentrates on Nash equilibria; as \(\beta \to 0\), \(\pi_\beta\) approaches the uniform distribution.

Convergence demonstration. We run the same model from opposite starting densities and verify convergence toward similar equilibrium configurations:

set.seed(42)

M_conv <- 4; N_conv <- 5; iters_conv <- 30

sm_conv <- list(
  dv_bipartite = list(
    name = DV_NAME,
    effects = list(
      list(effect = "density", parameter = -0.5, dv_name = DV_NAME, fix = TRUE),
      list(effect = "inPop",   parameter = 0.15, dv_name = DV_NAME, fix = TRUE)
    ),
    coDyadCovars = list(
      list(
        effect = "XWX", parameter = 0.2, dv_name = DV_NAME, fix = TRUE,
        nodeSet = c("COMPONENTS", "COMPONENTS"),
        interaction1 = "self$component_1_coDyadCovar",
        x = create_block_diag(N_conv, round(N_conv / 2))
      )
    )
  )
)

## Sparse start (BI_PROB = 0.1)
env_sparse <- SaomNkRSienaBiEnv$new(list(
  M = M_conv, N = N_conv, BI_PROB = 0.1,
  rand_seed = 100, name = "_sparse_start_"
))
env_sparse$search_rsiena(sm_conv, iterations_per_actor = iters_conv, run_seed = 200)

## Dense start (BI_PROB = 0.8)
env_dense <- SaomNkRSienaBiEnv$new(list(
  M = M_conv, N = N_conv, BI_PROB = 0.8,
  rand_seed = 101, name = "_dense_start_"
))
env_dense$search_rsiena(sm_conv, iterations_per_actor = iters_conv, run_seed = 201)

## Compare final densities
dens_sparse <- sum(env_sparse$bipartite_matrix) / (M_conv * N_conv)
dens_dense  <- sum(env_dense$bipartite_matrix)  / (M_conv * N_conv)

cat("Sparse start (0.10) --> Final density:", round(dens_sparse, 3), "\n")
#> Sparse start (0.10) --> Final density: 0.6
cat("Dense  start (0.80) --> Final density:", round(dens_dense, 3), "\n")
#> Dense  start (0.80) --> Final density: 0.7
cat("\nBoth converge toward a similar equilibrium density,\n")
#> 
#> Both converge toward a similar equilibrium density,
cat("regardless of initial conditions. This is Blume's result in action.\n")
#> regardless of initial conditions. This is Blume's result in action.

3.4.1 Bounded Rationality Spectrum

\(\beta\) Behavior NK Equivalent
\(0\) Random search (uniform over actions) —
\((0, \infty)\) Noisy best response (logit QRE) —
\(\to \infty\) Greedy deterministic choice NK adaptive walk

The intermediate regime \(\beta \in (0, \infty)\) has no NK analogue—it is a genuinely new behavioral domain enabled by the SaoMNK generalization.

4 Appendix D: NK Validation (Levinthal 1997 Reproduction)

This appendix validates the SaoMNK framework against canonical results from the NK fitness landscape literature.

4.1 Single-Agent Rugged Landscape

In the classical NK model, ruggedness is governed by \(K\). Levinthal (1997) showed that higher \(K\) increases local optima and traps the agent at suboptimal peaks. SaoMNK reproduces this with \(M=2\), \(N=8\), and modular epistasis:

epistasis_nk <- create_block_diag(8, 2)

env_rugged <- SaomNkRSienaBiEnv$new(list(
  M = 2, N = 8, BI_PROB = 0, rand_seed = 42,
  name = "_nk_rugged_"
))

sm_rugged <- list(
  dv_bipartite = list(
    name = DV_NAME,
    effects = list(
      list(effect = "density", parameter = -1.5, dv_name = DV_NAME, fix = TRUE)
    ),
    coCovars = list(), varCovars = list(),
    coDyadCovars = list(
      list(
        effect = "XWX", parameter = 1.5, dv_name = DV_NAME, fix = TRUE,
        nodeSet = c("COMPONENTS", "COMPONENTS"),
        interaction1 = "self$component_1_coDyadCovar",
        x = epistasis_nk
      )
    ),
    varDyadCovars = list()
  )
)

env_rugged$search_rsiena(sm_rugged, iterations_per_actor = 30, run_seed = 12345)
env_rugged$plot_degree_4panel(loess_span = 0.5)

4.2 Multi-Agent Endogenous Landscape

With \(M=6\) and endogenous effects activated, \(K_{AA}\) (actor sociality) and \(K_{CC}\) (component epistasis) emerge from the coupled bipartite process:

env_endog <- SaomNkRSienaBiEnv$new(list(
  M = 6, N = 8, BI_PROB = 0, rand_seed = 99,
  name = "_nk_multi_endog_"
))

sm_endog <- list(
  dv_bipartite = list(
    name = DV_NAME,
    effects = list(
      list(effect = "density", parameter = -1.0, dv_name = DV_NAME, fix = TRUE),
      list(effect = "inPop",   parameter = 0.2,  dv_name = DV_NAME, fix = TRUE),
      list(effect = "outAct",  parameter = 0.1,  dv_name = DV_NAME, fix = TRUE)
    ),
    coCovars = list(), varCovars = list(),
    coDyadCovars = list(
      list(
        effect = "XWX", parameter = 1.0, dv_name = DV_NAME, fix = TRUE,
        nodeSet = c("COMPONENTS", "COMPONENTS"),
        interaction1 = "self$component_1_coDyadCovar",
        x = epistasis_nk
      )
    ),
    varDyadCovars = list()
  )
)

env_endog$search_rsiena(sm_endog, iterations_per_actor = 30, run_seed = 12345)
env_endog$plot_degree_4panel(loess_span = 0.3)

With endogenous effects active, the K-4 panel shows coupled dynamics: density pressure constrains \(K_{AC}\), preferential attachment generates heterogeneous \(K_{CA}\), and the emergent \(K_{CC}\) is no longer a free parameter but a structural consequence of actors’ affiliation choices.

4.3 Parameter Mapping Table

NK Parameter SaoMNK Mapping Effect
\(N\) (components) N Number of binary components
\(K\) (epistasis) XWX matrix structure Block-diagonal \(\to\) modular; full \(\to\) \(K = N-1\)
Single agent M = 2 (SaoMNK minimum) Single active searcher
Fixed landscape \(\theta = \mathbf{0}\) No endogenous network effects
Greedy search \(\beta \to \infty\) Deterministic best-response
Ruggedness density magnitude More negative \(\to\) costlier exploration

5 Appendix E: Simulation Walkthrough

This appendix demonstrates the full simulation workflow: heterogeneous actor strategies, exogenous shocks, and multi-wave execution.

5.1 Actor Strategies with Heterogeneous Covariates

Actors can be assigned to different strategy groups using coCovars, where each group has different weights on the network statistics:

env_strat <- SaomNkRSienaBiEnv$new(list(
  M = 6, N = 8, BI_PROB = 0, rand_seed = 1234, name = "_strategy_demo_"
))

## Two strategy dimensions assigned cyclically
strategies <- list(
  egoX   = c(-1, 0, 1),
  inPopX = c( 1, 0, -1)
)
actor_strats <- lapply(strategies, function(s) rep(s, length.out = 6))

epistasis_strat <- create_block_diag(8, round(8 / 3))

sm_strat <- list(
  dv_bipartite = list(
    name = DV_NAME,
    effects = list(
      list(effect = "density", parameter = -0.3, dv_name = DV_NAME, fix = TRUE),
      list(effect = "inPop",   parameter =  0.2, dv_name = DV_NAME, fix = TRUE),
      list(effect = "outAct",  parameter =  0.1, dv_name = DV_NAME, fix = TRUE)
    ),
    coCovars = list(
      list(effect = "egoX", parameter = 0.2, dv_name = DV_NAME, fix = TRUE,
           interaction1 = "self$strat_1_coCovar",
           x = actor_strats[[1]]),
      list(effect = "inPopX", parameter = 0.2, dv_name = DV_NAME, fix = TRUE,
           interaction1 = "self$strat_2_coCovar",
           x = actor_strats[[2]])
    ),
    varCovars = list(),
    coDyadCovars = list(
      list(effect = "XWX", parameter = 0.02, dv_name = DV_NAME, fix = TRUE,
           nodeSet = c("COMPONENTS", "COMPONENTS"),
           interaction1 = "self$component_1_coDyadCovar",
           x = epistasis_strat)
    ),
    varDyadCovars = list(), interactions = list()
  )
)

env_strat$search_rsiena(sm_strat, iterations = env_strat$M * 30, run_seed = 12345)
env_strat$plot_degree_4panel(loess_span = 0.25)

5.2 Exogenous Shocks via theta_shocks

The theta_shocks mechanism models exogenous events (regulatory changes, technology disruptions) by modifying SAOM parameters at a designated step:

env_base <- SaomNkRSienaBiEnv$new(list(
  M = 6, N = 8, BI_PROB = 0, rand_seed = 42, name = "_baseline_"
))

sm_base <- list(
  dv_bipartite = list(
    name = DV_NAME,
    effects = list(
      list(effect = "density", parameter = -0.5, dv_name = DV_NAME, fix = TRUE)
    ),
    coDyadCovars = list(
      list(effect = "XWX", parameter = 0.5, dv_name = DV_NAME, fix = TRUE,
           nodeSet = c("COMPONENTS", "COMPONENTS"),
           interaction1 = "self$component_1_coDyadCovar",
           x = create_block_diag(8, 2))
    )
  )
)

## Baseline (no shock)
env_base$search_rsiena(sm_base, iterations_per_actor = 30, run_seed = 12345)
env_base$plot_degree_4panel(loess_span = 0.3)

## Shocked simulation: density drops from -0.5 to -2.0 at midpoint
env_shocked <- SaomNkRSienaBiEnv$new(list(
  M = 6, N = 8, BI_PROB = 0, rand_seed = 42, name = "_shocked_"
))

theta_shocks <- list(
  list(
    effect_level = c("density_dv_bipartite"),
    new_parameter = c(-2.0),
    portion = 1
  )
)

shock_ok <- tryCatch({
  env_shocked$search_rsiena(
    sm_base,
    iterations_per_actor = 30,
    run_seed = 12345,
    theta_shocks = theta_shocks
  )
  TRUE
}, error = function(e) {
  cat("Shock note:", e$message, "\n")
  FALSE
})
if (exists("shock_ok") && shock_ok) {
  env_shocked$plot_degree_4panel(loess_span = 0.3)
} else {
  cat("Shock simulation did not complete; see note above.\n")
}

The structural break in the K-4 trajectories at the shock step demonstrates how exogenous parameter changes propagate through the coupled search system.

6 Appendix F: Causal Inference Pipeline

The theta_shocks mechanism generates panel data suitable for quasi-experimental analysis. The searchnet_causal_panel() function extracts actor-level outcome trajectories indexed by (actor_id, chain_step_id), mapping directly to three causal inference designs.

Design Package When to Use
Difference-in-Differences did Multiple treated and control actors
Synthetic Control Synth Single treated actor; data-driven counterfactual
Regression Discontinuity rdrobust Sharp change at the shock step

6.1 Setting Up a Shocked Simulation

env_ci <- SaomNkRSienaBiEnv$new(list(
  M = 6, N = 8, BI_PROB = 0, rand_seed = 42, name = "_causal_"
))

K_ci <- create_block_diag(8, 2)

sm_ci <- list(
  dv_bipartite = list(
    name = DV_NAME,
    effects = list(
      list(effect = "density", parameter = -0.5, dv_name = DV_NAME, fix = TRUE)
    ),
    coDyadCovars = list(
      list(effect = "XWX", parameter = 0.5, dv_name = DV_NAME, fix = TRUE,
           nodeSet = c("COMPONENTS", "COMPONENTS"),
           interaction1 = "self$component_1_coDyadCovar",
           x = K_ci)
    )
  )
)

ci_shocks <- list(
  list(
    effect_level = c("density_dv_bipartite"),
    new_parameter = c(-2.0),
    portion = 1
  )
)

ci_ok <- tryCatch({
  env_ci$search_rsiena(sm_ci, iterations_per_actor = 20, run_seed = 12345,
                       theta_shocks = ci_shocks)
  TRUE
}, error = function(e) {
  cat("Causal setup note:", e$message, "\n")
  FALSE
})

6.2 DID Example

## Requires the 'did' package (Callaway & Sant'Anna, 2021)
panel_did <- searchnet_causal_panel(
  env_ci, shock_step = round(max(env_ci$actor_util_df$chain_step_id) / 2),
  outcome = "utility", treated_actors = c(1, 2, 3)
)

att <- searchnet_did(panel_did)
summary(att)
p <- searchnet_causal_plot(att, type = "did")
print(p)

6.3 Synthetic Control Example

## Requires the 'Synth' package
panel_sc <- searchnet_causal_panel(
  env_ci, shock_step = round(max(env_ci$actor_util_df$chain_step_id) / 2),
  outcome = "utility", treated_actors = c(1)
)

sc_result <- searchnet_synth(panel_sc, treated_unit = 1)
p <- searchnet_causal_plot(sc_result, type = "synth")
print(p)

6.4 Regression Discontinuity Example

## Requires the 'rdrobust' package
panel_rd <- searchnet_causal_panel(
  env_ci, shock_step = round(max(env_ci$actor_util_df$chain_step_id) / 2),
  outcome = "utility"
)

rd_result <- searchnet_rd(panel_rd)
summary(rd_result$rd)
p <- searchnet_causal_plot(rd_result, type = "rd")
print(p)

All three methods also work with K-4 outcomes (K_AC, K_CA, K_AA, K_CC), enabling researchers to analyze the causal effect of shocks on specific dimensions of the coupled degree system.

7 Appendix G: Blume Convergence and Gibbs Measures

This appendix summarizes the theoretical foundation for Theorem 4 and demonstrates convergence computationally.

7.1 Potential Games

A game is an exact potential game (Monderer and Shapley, 1996) if there exists a single function \(\Phi(\mathbf{x})\) such that every player’s marginal utility from changing strategy equals the marginal change in the potential:

\[u_i(\mathbf{x}_{-i}, a'_i) - u_i(\mathbf{x}_{-i}, a_i) = \Phi(\mathbf{x}_{-i}, a'_i) - \Phi(\mathbf{x}_{-i}, a_i)\]

SAOMs with additive objective functions and symmetric statistics satisfy this condition, admitting a potential function \(\Phi(\mathbf{B}) = \sum_k \theta_k S_k(\mathbf{B})\).

7.2 Gibbs Measure and Phase Transitions

The Gibbs measure assigns probability to each configuration proportional to the exponential of its potential, with \(\beta\) controlling the sharpness:

\[\pi_\beta(\mathbf{x}) = \frac{\exp(\beta \cdot \Phi(\mathbf{x}))}{Z(\beta)}, \quad Z(\beta) = \sum_{\mathbf{x}'} \exp(\beta \cdot \Phi(\mathbf{x}'))\]

The parameter \(\beta\) acts as an inverse temperature:

\(\beta\) (Rationality) Temperature Behavior
\(\beta = 0\) \(T \to \infty\) Uniform distribution (random search)
\(\beta = 1\) \(T = 1\) Moderate exploration
\(\beta \to \infty\) \(T \to 0\) Concentration on Nash equilibria

7.3 Blume’s Theorem (Logit–Gibbs Convergence)

For a finite potential game with potential function \(\Phi\), if players revise strategies via asynchronous logit best response with \(\beta > 0\), then the induced Markov chain is ergodic and has a unique stationary distribution equal to the Gibbs measure \(\pi_\beta\).

The proof rests on detailed balance: for any two configurations \(\mathbf{x}\), \(\mathbf{x}'\) differing in one player’s strategy,

\[\frac{P(\mathbf{x} \to \mathbf{x}')}{P(\mathbf{x}' \to \mathbf{x})} = \frac{\exp(\beta \cdot \Phi(\mathbf{x}'))}{\exp(\beta \cdot \Phi(\mathbf{x}))} = \frac{\pi_\beta(\mathbf{x}')}{\pi_\beta(\mathbf{x})}\]

The first equality follows from the logit rule, the second from the potential game property, confirming detailed balance.

7.4 Convergence Demonstration

We run the same model from sparse and dense starting points to demonstrate that both converge toward the same equilibrium:

## Already computed in Appendix C (Theorem 4 verification)
## Reuse the sparse and dense environments

## Side-by-side K-4 panels
par(mfrow = c(1, 2))
env_sparse$plot_actor_degrees(loess_span = 0.4)

env_dense$plot_actor_degrees(loess_span = 0.4)

par(mfrow = c(1, 1))

Both simulations—starting from nearly empty (density 0.10) and nearly full (density 0.80) bipartite networks—converge toward similar degree distributions, confirming the independence from initial conditions predicted by Blume’s theorem.

8 Appendix H: Computational Performance

8.1 Overhead Relative to RSiena

searchnet adds 15–25% overhead relative to a raw RSiena simulation of equivalent size. The majority is attributable to chain statistics extraction and K-4 degree computation. The projection operations are \(O(M^2 N)\) and \(O(M N^2)\) respectively, dominated by the RSiena simulation cost for \(M, N \lesssim 50\).

time_sn <- system.time({
  e_b <- SaomNkRSienaBiEnv$new(list(
    M = 4, N = 6, BI_PROB = 0, rand_seed = 1, name = "_bench_"
  ))
  sm_b <- list(
    dv_bipartite = list(
      name = DV_NAME,
      effects = list(
        list(effect = "density", parameter = -0.5, dv_name = DV_NAME, fix = TRUE)
      ),
      coDyadCovars = list(
        list(effect = "XWX", parameter = 0.5, dv_name = DV_NAME, fix = TRUE,
             nodeSet = c("COMPONENTS", "COMPONENTS"),
             interaction1 = "self$component_1_coDyadCovar",
             x = create_block_diag(6, 2))
      )
    )
  )
  e_b$search_rsiena(sm_b, iterations_per_actor = 30, run_seed = 1)
})

cat(sprintf("searchnet (M=4, N=6, 30 steps/actor): %.2fs elapsed\n",
            time_sn["elapsed"]))
#> searchnet (M=4, N=6, 30 steps/actor): 1.40s elapsed

8.2 Scalability Table

Median wall-clock times for search_rsiena() with 30 steps per actor, based on the manuscript benchmarks (Intel Core i7-13700K, 64 GB RAM, R 4.3.2):

\(M\) \(N\) Time (s)
6 8 0.8
10 15 2.1
12 20 4.3
20 30 12.7
20 40 24.5
30 50 58.2

Scaling is approximately quadratic in \(N\) and linear in \(M\).

8.3 Fitness Landscape Enumeration

The compute_fitness_landscape() method enumerates all \(2^N\) configurations. This is \(O(2^N)\) and feasible for \(N \leq 20\). For \(N = 12\): ~0.3s; for \(N = 20\): ~45s. For larger \(N\), an MCMC sampling approximation (default \(S = 10{,}000\) draws) estimates landscape statistics without full enumeration.

Multi-agent Yes (\(M \geq 2\)) No Yes
Endogenous \(K\) Yes (\(\{K\}\) framework) No No

Causal inference Yes (DID, SC, RD) No No
